records.name: Algeria
records.summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised, but Cairo 52 documents that it is effectively criminalised through Penal Code Articles 333, 338, and 333 bis (indecency provisions), and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these articles. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years under Article 338. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 country page (Algeria): NGOs document arrests within the LGBT+ community with little information on the trans identity of those arrested; no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare — arts. 274/264 could be used against providers (de facto criminalisation); no legal gender-recognition route, so civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked.

UK Home Office CPIN 'Algeria: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression' (26 Jul 2026, covering since May 2025): same-sex activity prohibited under Penal Code 1966 ('acts of homosexuality', Human Dignity Trust updated June 2026); internal relocation viable for gay males but lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties; refusals rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded — the current asylum-authority baseline.

Snopes fact-check (5 Aug 2024): Rating TRUE — Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and being transgender; published while debunking the false Imane Khelif 'trans boxer' rumour, confirming the ban is real even though the rumour about the athlete was false.

US State Dept 2023 Country Reports (Algeria): law criminalised undefined 'homosexual acts' with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment plus fines; prison authorities separated vulnerable persons but LGBTQI+ detainees had no specific legal protections; civil society noted compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons.

ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia 2008: Algeria — male/male and female/female relations illegal under Penal Code (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966): 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. Dated but the same Penal Code 1966 that the 2026 CPIN confirms is still in force.

Human Rights Watch (15 Oct 2020): after a 24 Jul 2020 raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, police arrested 44 people (9 women, 35 men, mostly university students) over an alleged 'gay wedding'; on 3 Sep 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and 42 to suspended terms, using decorations and 'gay appearance' as evidence.

BBC/Arab Barometer (23 Jun 2019, 25,000 respondents across 10 countries + Palestinian territories): Algeria was the exception where fewer than 50% accepted a woman head of state; region-wide, 'not religious' identification rose from 8% to 13% since 2013 — social-conservatism context datum for the record.

records.name: Ethiopia
records.summary:
Ethiopia is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. The 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner than Cameroon's or Tunisia's — Ethiopia's LGBTQ+ community (self-identified as “zega”) is deeply underground, and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation + no LGR catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection place it clearly on the dangerous side of the scale. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the UPR reporting.

sources.summary: Stakeholder submission to Ethiopia's UPR (47th session): same-sex activity criminalised, leaving LGBTQ+ people at serious risk of harm and systematic exclusion; discrimination, violence, lack of police protection and stigma in services; no legal gender change - trans men are legally women and trans women legally men, so trans people in different-gender relationships can fall foul of the same-sex conduct law.

Stakeholder UPR report by The Advocates for Human Rights and House of Guramayle (April 2024) on SOGIE in Ethiopia: documents discrimination, violence, and lack of protection; notes transgender people are particularly at risk given the criminalisation framework.

F&M Global Barometers country profile, time series 2011-2024 (all years scored 'no' on every protection axis): no legal gender recognition (neither surgical nor psychiatric pathway exists), no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no freedom from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity/expression, LGBTI organisations cannot register, Pride events not allowed and participants unprotected, no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protections including gender identity. National LGBTI organisations exist despite the ban on registration.
US State Department 2008 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): documents the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma - baseline country-of-origin information.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia (archived): documents arrests of opposition figures, CSO-law restrictions on civil society, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Ethiopia: documents the anti-terrorism prosecutions, CSO-law restrictions, torture, harsh prisons - general context with the LGBT section noting criminalisation.

Lund University master's thesis (2009) by Daniel Iddo Balcha: 'Homosexuality in Ethiopia' - analyses the construction of homosexuality in relation to gender and feminism; male homosexuality criminalised (up to 3 years); media and elite create homophobia in discourse; the church effectively campaigns hatred; female homosexuality simply overlooked; attitudes shifting under globalisation.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code outlaws same-sex conduct between men and between women — rarely enforced but underpinning pervasive anti-LGBTIQ stigma, harassment and violence; in August 2023 security forces cracked down on 'homosexuality' while non-state actors drove an online incitement wave ending in physical attacks; Christian and Muslim groups campaign for harsher penalties (Orthodox Church declared its stance June 2024). Charities & Societies Proclamation Art 69 blocks registration of LGBTI groups as 'contrary to public morality'. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal nationwide, no legal gender recognition, LGBTI orgs cannot register.

records.name: Venezuela
records.summary:
Venezuela demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

The capital, Caracas, has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (10 Sep 2024): LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after the disputed July 2024 election; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 Sep 2024 -- persecution of LGBTQ people tied to the political crisis, dated.

EUAA asylum country-focus (reference period through 2025): dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of conditions in Venezuela used for international protection decisions -- the EU asylum agency's factual baseline on how LGBTIQ+ people are treated.
NOTE: The AFS/Vance Center LGBTQ guide on Venezuela (Oct 2024) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

Sydney Morning Herald (8 Aug 2015): Tamara Adrian, Venezuela's first transgender candidate, ran for the National Assembly -- landmark trans political candidacy under Venezuela's gender-recognition law context.

Cronica Uno poll (2-3 Mar 2023): a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% know the LGBTIQ+ term (13% do not); 36% think gay/lesbian/bisexuality is innate -- dated public-opinion data.

Blog record (31 Jan 2014): an equal-marriage bill was set to be presented to Venezuela's National Assembly that week (per Aporrea) -- legislative push for same-sex marriage, historic milestone (no later enactment recorded).

El Mundo (13 Dec 2015): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla -- Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian -- a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell -- state persecution of an openly gay politician.

records.name: Bolivia
records.summary:
Bolivia is workable for trans visitors — on paper a legal pioneer within this region. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (an administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. The constitution also names gender identity.

Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside the two largest cities (La Paz and Santa Cruz); and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.

sources.summary: Comparative Politics article (April 2024) 'Activists, Parties, and the Expansion of Trans Rights in Bolivia': Bolivia prohibits gender-identity discrimination and passed a ground-breaking gender identity law (2016, allowing name/marker change) despite low voter support; trans activists leveraged access to ruling-party legislators; contradictory heteronormative laws passed alongside because both organised religion and LGBT activists were party constituents.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (WordPress critical error); the underlying Agencia Presentes article (Dec 2024) covers Bolivia's first virtual survey revealing the great exclusion of LGBTI people.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Bolivia: general human-rights assessment (arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, corruption) - the LGBT section documents the constitutional anti-discrimination guarantee and societal discrimination.

Newsweek (Jul 2017): after the US trans military ban, only 18 countries are believed to fully legalise LGBT military service — international baseline for whether trans visitors/soldiers face service exclusion; Bolivia not singled out in the text.

Legal-profile page: Constitution prohibits discrimination and guarantees bodily integrity (Art 15(II) violence, 45(V) maternity), Penal Code Title VIII governs abortion. Superseded by post-2016 law: 2016 gender-identity law (self-ID), Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion, Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition for same-sex couples.

eju.tv/La Razón (25 Aug 2014, Spanish): homosexuality is taboo in Bolivia's armed forces — gay soldiers report discrimination and sanctions, testimony given anonymously; the TLGB collective and human-rights activists demand openness.

records.name: Paraguay
records.summary:
Paraguay demands real caution from trans visitors — the most conservative country in its region. There is no legal gender recognition (ten lawsuits on trans name recognition remain pending, unresolved), no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. AP documents that many LGBTQ+ people feel compelled to leave their hometowns due to discrimination, harassment, and gender-based violence; trans women face particular social rejection. Amnesty reports persistent structural discrimination and high gender-based violence.

Nothing criminalises being trans, the capital, Asunción, has a small organised community, and there is no documented police targeting pattern — the risk is social hostility and a total protection vacuum rather than state persecution. Tourist traffic is low and there are no documented trans-visitor incidents.

sources.summary: AP (Sep 2025): 'For Paraguay's transgender women, survival often means leaving home' — discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of hometowns into migration and sex work.

Amnesty International Paraguay page (2025-26): trans people face obstacles to legal identity-document recognition - two trans migrants were denied identity documents; Asuncion's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March; plus 37 registered feminicides in 2025 and April's bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

ecoi / US State Dept reporting: judiciary had yet to issue final rulings on 10 lawsuits filed by trans people for legal name recognition - plaintiffs Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepulveda (suits since 2016) awaited a UN Human Rights Committee decision on their ICCPR Optional Protocol communications. Documented pace of recognition litigation.

PinkNews (20 Oct 2017): political climate report - ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes said he would 'shoot himself in the testicles' if his son married another man (later apologised to those offended); frames the report's account of a push to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'. Elite-level anti-LGBT rhetoric.

Tico Times (10 Jan 2018): on the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage - notes Bolivia, Paraguay and Peru recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions, i.e. the ruling binds Paraguay (OAS party) though local law lagged; ~300 Costa Ricans celebrated at the court. Inter-American framework applying to Paraguay.

ABC Color (30 May 2017): adoption analysis - Law 1136/97 does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or singles from adopting (prohibitions cover only infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records), a legal gap allowing same-sex adoption as couples or as single men/women, amid a society that still closes doors. Adoption-law reality check.

Ultima Hora: post-IACtHR ruling analysis says people in Paraguay must overcome difficulties adapting the country's laws to extend the right to marriage to everyone - the domestic-law gap the inter-American opinion leaves for Paraguay to close.

records.name: Guatemala
records.summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group such as Lambda, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

sources.summary: Wikipedia article on transfemicide: documents killings of trans women; for Guatemala records that Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections — Guatemalan officials have justified this by stating that transgender women are not 'biological women' — the official exclusion underpinning the record's violence context.

Arcus Foundation report (May 2024): the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, but a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four countries.

HRW (Jan 2022): 'Guatemala: Anti-Trans Bill Threatens Rights' — documents legislative attacks on trans people, including bills that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Washington Blade (Jan 2018): Latin American countries including Guatemala urged to abide by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruling (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) requiring marriage equality and gender recognition — compliance status uncertain.
